environmentalPersistence: Extremely high — soil half-life 2–15 years; DDE and DDD metabolites persist for decades; still detectable globally despite bans

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Moderate — lipophilic accumulation in membranes impairs cell function broadly
morphologicalEffects.leafCurl: Moderate — membrane disruption causes structural changes
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Moderate — lipid-mediated membrane damage causes tissue death
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Moderately inhibited — highly lipophilic; accumulates in root cell membranes
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Old leaves show chlorosis first; new growth impaired over time

physiologyEffects.membranePermeability: Strongly increased — extreme lipophilicity disrupts all lipid bilayers

molecularEffects.oxidativeStress: Moderate — membrane disruption generates secondary ROS
molecularEffects.lipidPeroxidation: Strong — extremely lipophilic; partitions into membranes causing peroxidation

microbiomeEffects.diversityReduction: Strong — DDT persists in soil and continues suppressing microbiome for years
microbiomeEffects.beneficialBacteriaEffect: Strongly suppressed — DDT accumulates in bacterial cell membranes
microbiomeEffects.fungalEffect: Strongly disrupted — mycorrhizal associations severely impaired
microbiomeEffects.rhizosphereStability: Severely and persistently destabilized — decades-long effect

temporalDynamics.firstSymptomsHours: 72–168 hours — slower than more water-soluble compounds
temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: None — DDT does not degrade on plant-relevant timescales; accumulates continuously
temporalDynamics.sensitization: Accumulative — lipophilic bioaccumulation causes worsening symptoms over weeks

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Slow progression from green → mildly chlorotic; dark spots from lipid deposit accumulation
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Uniform mild chlorosis — less dramatic visually than herbicides; the story is the persistence and bioaccumulation
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Moderate — DDE accumulation signature is persistent; doesn't decay over 6 weeks unlike most chemicals
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Progressive reduction over 6 weeks; near-zero by week 6; resistome elevated
visualSimulation.recoveryVisual: No recovery — DDT accumulates in tissue; continued slow deterioration

synergies.synergyNote: Historical use of organochlorine + organophosphate mixtures; combined lipophilic membrane disruption and AChE inhibition produce synergistic microbiome collapse

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Historical agricultural/public health use; banned in US 1972 and most countries; still used for malaria control in some tropical countries; globally persistent — detectable in Arctic wildlife and deep ocean sediments
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: Banned in most countries; ~4,000 tonnes/year still produced for malaria vector control in limited countries
educationalContext.humanToxicity: High — carcinogen; endocrine disruptor; causes eggshell thinning in birds (brought bald eagle near extinction); linked to breast cancer and diabetes
educationalContext.climateLink: DDT is a persistent organic pollutant that concentrates in Arctic ecosystems — climate-driven melting of polar ice releases DDT stored for decades back into the food chain
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Outdoor — historical agricultural; current use indoor/outdoor for malaria control in Africa and Asia
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring — the book that started the modern environmental movement. DDT nearly drove the bald eagle extinct. Still present in the environment 50+ years after the US ban.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Persistent organic pollutants, bioaccumulation in food chains, DDT and malaria tradeoffs, polar pollutant transport
